verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Snare and a Net
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Priests, people and king are summoned: the judgment is for you, for they have been a snare and a net (vv. 1-2). God knows Ephraim (v. 3). Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for the spirit of whoredom is within them (v. 4). They will seek the LORD with flocks and herds but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin binds people so that they cannot return, and ritual without repentance cannot find God.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O priests! Pay attention, O house of Israel! Give ear, O house of the king! For the judgment is for you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor. And the revolters have gone deep into slaughter, but I will discipline all of them. I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore; Israel is defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, O priests! Pay attention, O house of Israel! Give ear, O house of the king! For the judgment is for you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor.

Three groups are called to court: the priests, the house of Israel (the people) and the house of the king. Religious leaders, ordinary people and rulers are all guilty together.

They have been a snare and a net, like hunters' traps. Mizpah and Tabor were places on either side of the Jordan, perhaps sites of worship or royal authority. The places that should have drawn people to God had become traps that caught them in idolatry. Leaders who should protect God's people can become the very ones who lead them into sin.

And the revolters have gone deep into slaughter, but I will discipline all of them.

I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore; Israel is defiled.

I know Ephraim. Israel had lost the knowledge of God (4:1), but God had not lost his knowledge of Israel. Nothing was hidden. That truth is a terror for those who hide their sin, and a comfort for those who long to be fully known and still loved.

verseByVerse.quote: Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. For the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the LORD. The pride of Israel testifies to his face; Israel and Ephraim shall stumble in his guilt; Judah also shall stumble with them. With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them. They have dealt faithlessly with the LORD; for they have borne alien children. Now the new moon shall devour them with their fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. For the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the LORD.

This is one of the most sobering verses in the book. Their deeds do not permit them to return. Sin is not only something we do. It becomes something that holds us. The more they sinned, the less able they were to turn back. The spirit of whoredom is within them. Jesus said, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). No one should imagine they can live in sin for years and then easily turn back whenever they choose. Only God's grace can break that grip.

The pride of Israel testifies to his face; Israel and Ephraim shall stumble in his guilt; Judah also shall stumble with them.

Israel's pride stands up in court as a witness against it. (The ESV notes that to his face may mean "in his presence".) And Judah, which was warned in 4:15, will fall too.

With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them.

Here is the tragedy of religion without repentance. They will bring animals to sacrifice. They will seek the LORD. But they will not find him. Why not? Because they wanted God's help without giving up their sin. Isaiah heard God say the same: What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? (Isa 1:11). God cannot be bought with offerings. He can only be found by those who turn to him with their whole heart.

They have dealt faithlessly with the LORD; for they have borne alien children. Now the new moon shall devour them with their fields.

Alien children may refer to children born of the fertility cult, or to a generation raised as strangers to God. Either way, the parents' unfaithfulness had produced children who did not belong to God. The new moon, a religious festival day, will not bring blessing but judgment on their harvests.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds in the towns of Benjamin (v. 8). Ephraim will become a desolation, and Judah's leaders, like landmark-movers, face God's wrath (vv. 9-11). God is like a moth and dry rot to them (v. 12). When they saw their sickness, they went to Assyria, But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound (v. 13). God will be like a lion and tear (v. 14): I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people must not seek healing from the powers of the world; God withdraws so that they will seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven; we follow you, O Benjamin! Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of punishment; among the tribes of Israel I make known what is sure. The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water. Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven; we follow you, O Benjamin!

Suddenly the scene becomes a war. Alarm horns sound in Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven, towns in the territory of Benjamin, on the border between Israel and Judah. (The ESV notes that the last phrase may be "after you", a battle cry.)

Many think this describes the war of about 734-732 BC, when Israel joined with Syria to attack Judah, and Judah's King Ahaz called on Assyria for help (2 Kgs 16:5-9; Isa 7:1-2). The two halves of God's people were fighting each other, and both were about to be crushed by a foreign empire.

Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of punishment; among the tribes of Israel I make known what is sure.

The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water.

Moving a boundary stone was a way of stealing a neighbor's land, and God's law forbade it (Deut 19:14). The leaders of Judah were doing on a national scale what thieves did on a small one, grabbing territory in the chaos of war.

Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth.

Ephraim was determined to go its own way. (The ESV notes that filth may mean "to follow human precepts".) Its suffering was the result of a settled choice.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like dry rot to the house of Judah. When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to the great king. But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound. For I will be like a lion to Ephraim, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear and go away; I will carry off, and no one shall rescue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like dry rot to the house of Judah.

God describes his judgment with two quiet, frightening pictures. A moth eats through clothing unseen. Dry rot eats through wood from the inside. Nothing seems to happen, and then one day the garment falls apart or the beam gives way. God's judgment is not always sudden. Sometimes it is a slow decay that goes unnoticed until it is too late.

When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to the great king. But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound.

Both kingdoms finally noticed they were sick. But instead of turning to God, they went to Assyria, the superpower of the day. King Menahem of Israel paid Assyria a fortune in silver for support (2 Kgs 15:19-20), and King Ahaz of Judah begged, I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me (2 Kgs 16:7). (The ESV notes that the great king may be a name, "King Jareb".)

But he is not able to cure you. The world's powers cannot heal what is wrong with God's people. The same Assyria they ran to would destroy Israel. Every generation of believers is tempted to look for rescue in politics, money or human strength instead of in God. In returning and rest you shall be saved, God said through Isaiah, But you were unwilling (Isa 30:15).

For I will be like a lion to Ephraim, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear and go away; I will carry off, and no one shall rescue.

The moth becomes a lion. The slow decay turns into a sudden attack. And notice who the lion is. Not Assyria, but God: I, even I, will tear. Assyria would only be the instrument. Behind every judgment of history stands the Lord of history.

verseByVerse.quote: I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.

After tearing, the lion goes back to its den and waits. God withdraws. But the verse contains one word full of hope: until. God's absence has a purpose. He waits until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face.

Notice what God is waiting for. Not better sacrifices, not political alliances, but two things: confessing their guilt and seeking his face. In their distress earnestly seek me. God sometimes lets his people come to the end of themselves so that they will finally look for him.

That is exactly what the prodigal son did. When he came to himself, he said, I will arise and go to my father, and while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him (Luke 15:17-20). The God who withdraws is watching the road. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (Jas 4:8). The next chapter begins with the words he is waiting to hear: Come, let us return to the LORD.

5.title: Until They Seek My Face
5.overview:
Priests, the people of Israel and the royal house are called to judgment, for they have been a snare at Mizpah and a net on Tabor. God knows Ephraim and its defilement (vv. 1-3).

Their deeds keep them from returning to God, for a spirit of whoredom is within them and they do not know the LORD. Israel's pride testifies against it, and Israel, Ephraim and Judah will stumble. They will seek the LORD with their flocks and herds but will not find him, for he has withdrawn; they have been faithless and borne alien children (vv. 4-7).

The alarm is sounded at Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven. Ephraim will become a desolation; Judah's princes are like those who move landmarks, and God will pour out his wrath on them (vv. 8-11).

God is like a moth to Ephraim and dry rot to Judah. When they saw their sickness, they went to Assyria, but the great king could not heal them. God will be like a lion, tearing and carrying off with no one to rescue. Then he will return to his place until they acknowledge their guilt and earnestly seek his face (vv. 12-15).
5.theology:
Religious leaders, people and rulers are all accountable to God, and nothing is hidden from him (vv. 1-3).

Persistent sin enslaves, so that people cannot return to God without his grace (v. 4; John 8:34).

Religious ritual without repentance cannot find God (v. 6; Isa 1:11).

God's judgment may work slowly like decay or suddenly like a lion, and he stands behind the powers he uses (vv. 12, 14).

God's people must not seek from the world's powers the healing only God can give (v. 13; Isa 30:15).

God withdraws in order to bring his people to confess their guilt and seek his face, and he receives those who return (v. 15; Luke 15:17-20; Jas 4:8).
5.examples:
Places of worship turned into hunters' traps.

A people who could not return because their sins held them.

Worshippers who bring their flocks and cannot find God.

A moth in the closet and rot in the beams.

A sick nation asking the superpower for a cure.

A lion that tears and then waits in its den.

When I restore the fortunes of my people,

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up (v. 1). After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him (v. 2). Let us press on to know the LORD; he will come like the dawn and the spring rains (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him, and raises them up to live before him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up.

At the end of chapter 5 God said he would withdraw until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face (5:15). Now we hear words of return: Come, let us return to the LORD.

These words are beautiful, and they are exactly right. The God who tears is the God who heals. The lion of 5:14 is also the physician. He has torn us, that he may heal us. God's wounds are never meant to destroy his people but to bring them back. The same hand that strikes is the hand that binds up.

But who is speaking, and do they mean it? Christians have read these verses in two ways. Many believe they are the words of the people, a quick, easy repentance that assumes God will simply fix everything, and that God's sad reply in verse 4 shows it was not real. Others believe this is Hosea himself calling the people to genuine repentance, a pattern of what true return looks like. Both readings teach something important. The words are true. The question is whether they come from the heart. It is possible to say all the right things about returning to God and still not return.

verseByVerse.quote: After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him. Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD; his going out is sure as the dawn; he will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.

After two days... on the third day is a way of saying "very soon". Those speaking are confident that God's healing will come quickly, and that he will revive the nation, raising it up from its sickness as if from death, that we may live before him.

Many Christians have heard in this verse a pointer to something greater. Jesus said, Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead (Luke 24:46), and Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Cor 15:4). Neither passage names Hosea, and we should not claim more than the text says. But the pattern is striking. Israel hoped to be raised up on the third day to live before God. That hope was finally fulfilled in the one true Israelite, Jesus, who was raised on the third day, and in whom all who belong to him are raised to new life. Our hope of revival is not in our own quick repentance but in his resurrection.

Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD; his going out is sure as the dawn; he will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth."

The missing knowledge of God (4:1, 6) is exactly what they now long for: let us press on to know the LORD. And they are sure God will come, as sure as the sunrise, as refreshing as the spring rains that make the crops grow. Notice the contrast with Baal. They had worshipped Baal to get rain. The true rain comes from the LORD.

For Christians, this is a good prayer to make our own: let us press on to know the LORD. Knowing God is not a single moment but a lifelong pursuit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Your Love Is Like a Morning Cloud
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? Their love vanishes like the dew that goes early away (v. 4), so God has struck them through the prophets (v. 5). For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (v. 6). But like Adam they transgressed the covenant (v. 7); Gilead and the priests are stained with blood (vv. 8-10), and a harvest of judgment is appointed for Judah too (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God is not satisfied with religious ritual; he desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away. Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth as the light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away.

Now God answers, and his answer sounds like a heartbroken parent: What shall I do with you? God is not puzzled. He is grieved.

The problem is not that they never loved God. It is that their love does not last. It is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away. In the Middle East, a morning mist can promise rain, and dew covers everything at dawn. But when the sun rises, both are gone within an hour. Israel's repentance was like that: real feeling, gone by midmorning.

Many of us know this kind of love for God. A moving sermon, a crisis, a season of revival, and we are full of devotion. A week later it has evaporated. God does not want morning-dew religion. He wants steadfast love, love that lasts through the heat of the day. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation, Paul says, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor 7:10). The difference is whether it changes the heart.

Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth as the light.

Because their love was so shallow, God sent the prophets with words that cut like an axe. God's word is not only comfort. It wounds in order to heal. And God's judgment goes forth as the light. It is clear, open and impossible to escape.

verseByVerse.quote: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

This is perhaps the best-known verse in Hosea, and one of the most important in the Old Testament.

God does not reject sacrifice altogether. He commanded it. But he says that what he truly wants is steadfast love, loyal covenant love toward him and toward others, and the knowledge of God. Sacrifices without love and knowledge are worthless to him. Samuel said it long before: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). Micah said it after: what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (Mic 6:8). David understood it: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17).

Jesus quoted this verse twice. When the Pharisees criticized him for eating with tax collectors and sinners, he said, Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Matt 9:13). And when they condemned his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, he said, if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless (Matt 12:7). (Jesus' wording follows the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which, as the ESV notes, reads "mercy".)

Religious people are always tempted to think that God is pleased with correct ritual, church attendance and religious duties, while their hearts remain cold and their treatment of others is hard. God says no. What he desires is love for him and mercy toward people. And Christ himself fulfilled this verse perfectly. He offered the one sacrifice that truly pleased God, and he offered it out of steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me. Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood. As robbers lie in wait for a man, so the priests band together; they murder on the way to Shechem; they commit villainy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me.

This verse is debated. Some understand like Adam to refer to the first man. Just as Adam broke the command God gave him in Eden, Israel broke its covenant. Many Reformed theologians have pointed to this verse as evidence that God's relationship with Adam in the garden was a covenant. Others note the word there and think it refers to a place, the town called Adam by the Jordan, where Israel crossed into the land (Josh 3:16), perhaps the site of some act of unfaithfulness we no longer know. Both readings are possible.

Either way, the charge is clear: they transgressed the covenant. And if the first reading is right, it reminds us of something the whole Bible teaches. All humanity sinned in Adam. Israel's failure was the same failure repeated. That is why we need another Adam who would keep covenant perfectly, the one Paul calls the one who was to come (Rom 5:14), Jesus Christ.

Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood.

As robbers lie in wait for a man, so the priests band together; they murder on the way to Shechem; they commit villainy.

The examples are shocking. A town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, has blood on its streets. And the priests behave like a gang of highway robbers, ambushing travelers on the road to Shechem. Shechem was one of the cities of refuge, where people could flee for protection. The priests turned the road to safety into a place of murder. The people who should have been shepherds had become wolves.

verseByVerse.quote: In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; Ephraim's whoredom is there; Israel is defiled. For you also, O Judah, a harvest is appointed. When I restore the fortunes of my people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; Ephraim's whoredom is there; Israel is defiled.

God has seen it himself: a horrible thing. The unfaithfulness of his people is not a small matter to him. It horrifies him.

For you also, O Judah, a harvest is appointed. When I restore the fortunes of my people,

Judah too will reap what it has sown: a harvest is appointed. The last line, When I restore the fortunes of my people, begins a sentence that continues into chapter 7. Even in a chapter of judgment, God speaks of restoring his people. He has not given up. But first he must deal with their sin.

Chapter 6 holds together two truths we need. God truly heals those who return to him, and he raises them up to live before him. But he is not fooled by morning-dew religion. He desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself. The only one who has ever offered God both perfectly is Jesus Christ, and it is in him, crucified and raised on the third day, that we can return and live.

6.title: Steadfast Love and Not Sacrifice
6.overview:
"Come, let us return to the LORD," the call goes; he has torn and struck, and he will heal and bind up. After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up to live before him. Let us press on to know the LORD, whose coming is as sure as the dawn and the spring rains (vv. 1-3).

God asks what he should do with Ephraim and Judah, whose love is like a morning cloud and early dew. So he has hewn them by the prophets and slain them by his words. He desires steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (vv. 4-6).

Like Adam they transgressed the covenant and dealt faithlessly. Gilead is tracked with blood, and priests murder like robbers on the road to Shechem. God has seen a horrible thing in Israel. A harvest is appointed for Judah also, when God restores the fortunes of his people (vv. 7-11).
6.theology:
The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him (v. 1).

God revives his people and raises them up to live before him, a hope fulfilled in Christ, raised on the third day (v. 2; Luke 24:46; 1 Cor 15:4).

Knowing God is a lifelong pursuit (v. 3).

Shallow, passing devotion does not satisfy God; true repentance changes the heart (v. 4; 2 Cor 7:10).

God desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself more than religious ritual, as Jesus taught (v. 6; Matt 9:13; 12:7; 1 Sam 15:22; Mic 6:8; Ps 51:17).

Israel repeated Adam's covenant-breaking, and all humanity needs the last Adam, Jesus Christ (v. 7; Rom 5:14).
6.examples:
A lion that tears in order to heal.

A promise of rising on the third day.

Love that vanishes like morning mist.

A worshipper with perfect attendance and a cold heart.

Jesus eating with sinners and quoting Hosea.

Priests ambushing travelers on the road to a city of refuge.
